routes.label: Use midpoint reflection and a finite separation bound

question: Bela and Jenn play the following game on the closed interval \([0, n]\) of the real number line, where \(n\) is a fixed integer greater than \(4.\) They take turns playing, with Bela going first. At his first turn, Bela chooses any real number in the interval \([0, n].\) Thereafter, the player whose turn it is chooses a real number that is more than one unit away from all numbers previously chosen by either player. A player unable to choose such a number loses. Using optimal strategy, which player will win the game?
solution:
Choosing the midpoint leaves two matching halves of the interval. Bela can use that symmetry to pair every move Jenn makes with a legal reply.

Bela first chooses \(m=n/2\). Whenever Jenn chooses \(x\), Bela answers with \(y=n-x\), its reflection across \(m\). Since \(0\le x\le n\), the reply also belongs to \([0,n]\).

To verify legality, suppose the chosen numbers are symmetric about \(m\) before Jenn's turn. This is true initially, when only \(m\) has been chosen. For every previously chosen number \(z\), its reflection \(n-z\) has also been chosen. Jenn's legal move therefore satisfies
\[
|y-z|=|(n-x)-z|=|x-(n-z)|>1.
\]
Thus Bela's reply is more than one unit from every number chosen before Jenn's current move.

We must also compare the reply with Jenn's new number \(x\). Because \(m\) was already chosen, \(|x-m|>1\), and hence
\[
|y-x|=2|x-m|>2>1.
\]
So the reply is legal. Adding the reflected pair \(x,y\) restores symmetry for Jenn's next turn.

Finally, play cannot continue forever. If \(k\ge2\) chosen numbers are ordered as \(a_1<\cdots<a_k\), each consecutive gap exceeds \(1\). Adding these gaps gives
\[
k-1<a_k-a_1\le n.
\]
Since \(k\) and \(n\) are integers, \(k\le n\). Thus only finitely many moves are possible.

Bela can answer every legal Jenn move, so Jenn must be the first player unable to move. Therefore \(\boxed{\text{Bela will always win}}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
